title: Assessing the safety and value of shortened heart ultrasound scan protocols
official: The clinical utility of an abbreviated echocardiography protocol for the echocardiographic assessment of outpatients with aortic stenosis and inpatients post-acute coronary syndrome
summary:
Background and study aims 
This study will cover the area of abbreviated heart ultrasound scan protocols. This involves adapting and testing the current protocols we use during your scan against more focused scans that focus on specific cardiac conditions, in this case valve disease or left ventricular function. Some trials have attempted researching this topic in a more acute setting such as an emergency department or during the COVID era; however, only a handful of studies have researched the use of this protocol in routine outpatient care. We intend on testing the accuracy and safety of creating new focused protocols. This may help to reduce outpatient scan and clinic times, which may help to tackle both existing waiting lists for diagnosis and treatment while paving the way for more innovative services such as screening services for valve disease for community populations. We also aim to analyse the efficiency and cost savings of using such protocols. There will also be use of an automated AI software to interpret the images and a supplementary assessment of its accuracy.

Who can participate?
Patients aged 18 years and over with aortic stenosis or acute coronary syndrome

What does the study involve? 
You are due to have an echocardiogram as per your usual care; your involvement in this research study will only require additional images to be taken at the end of your routine scan. You will be eligible for this study if you are on a routine follow-up pathway to assess your heart valve disease.
The routine scan, which will be explained to you on the day of your appointment, will be as per usual protocol; it can take between 10 and 30 minutes. The additional images needed for the research study will require extra time; this will likely take an extra 5-10 minutes. 
The scan will require lying on your left side if physically possible; prolonged lying in this position may cause discomfort, but to resolve this, in between the routine scan and the additional images, you will be given a chance to stretch and have a break if you require. The same equipment will be used throughout, as the additional images are an extension of the routine scan. 
The additional set of images will be based upon a set protocol designed by the research team. It will essentially be a repeat scan of the one you would have already completed; however, it will not involve obtaining every image again, only a set few. 
The NHS sponsor holds appropriate insurance that applies to this study and confirms that compensation would be available in the event of harm. 

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
We hope to improve clinical and diagnostic guidance; the findings may help contribute to improving the efficiency of our echocardiography service and care for our patients in the future. 
You will need to be scanned twice as described above, which may mildly lengthen the scanning portion of your appointment. There are no perceived risks or harm associated with taking part in this study. 

Where is the study run from?
University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust (UK); it will also be run at a second site at Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
September 2026 to September 2028

Who is funding the study?
Investigator initiated and funded

Who is the study contact?

2. Dr Jeffrey Khoo, jeffrey.khoo@nhs.net
conditions: Aortic stenosis and acute coronary syndrome

interventions.name: Patients meeting the inclusion criteria will be approached for informed, written consent for the abbreviated research scan prior to their standard scan appointment. If they decline participation in the research study, they will go on to have only their standard clinical transthoracic echocardiogram

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Aortic stenosis cohort:
1. Provision of written informed consent 
2. Known aortic stenosis of any degree 
3. Must have had a prior baseline minimum standard echocardiogram dataset (BSE) at least 6 months ago
4. Outpatient or inpatient 

Acute coronary syndrome:
1. Provision of written informed consent 
2. Inpatient admitted with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) or unstable angina defined by two or more of raised cardiac troponin, ECG changes and/or symptoms as per European Society of Cardiology definitions
3. Outpatient if post-discharge without having an IP transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE)
4. Include MI with non-obstructive coronary artery (MINOCA)
5. Pre- and post-angiography patients will be included
6. Patients deemed to have Takotsubo cardiomyopathy will also be included
Exclusion criteria:
Aortic stenosis:
1. Unwilling or unable to provide written consent
2. Patient with other significant pathology on baseline echo which needs re-assessment (other valve disease, cardiomyopathies, etc)
3. Patient with poor echo views
4. Adult congenital heart disease (exception of bicuspid aortic valve)

Acute coronary syndrome cohort:
1. Unwilling or unable to provide written consent
2. Heart failure as primary diagnosis
3. Patients with known at least moderate severity of valve disease
